sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at, reverses_request_id | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id; reverses_request_id -> leave_requests.id | indexes: reverses_request_id: NEW column for GP-008. Unique (partial, non-null rows only) — a completed approval may be reversed at most once, which is the persistence-level guarantee that the balance release happens exactly once; also serves the lookup of a request's reversal row.; employee_id: role-scoped list/getById filter (employeeIds = ANY($n)) — EMPLOYEE sees own, MANAGER sees own + direct reports.; status: findByQuery status filter and lifecycle-state lookups (e.g. locating the APPROVED original).; leave_type_code, start_date: composite for leave-type + date-range queries and the ORDER BY start_date DESC list path.; employee_id, status: existing composite from the initial schema; retained for per-employee status listings.; approver_id: FK support for approver-scoped reads and referential integrity on delete/update of employees.; cancelled_by: FK support for cancellation-actor reads and referential integrity.

table leave_balances | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end, entitled_days, used_days, pending_days | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code | indexes: employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end: unique — findByKey resolves exactly one balance row per accrual period; the reversal's release targets this row.; employee_id: per-employee balance reads (GET /balances/me).

table audit_logs | fields: id, actor_id, action, entity_type, entity_id, before_state, after_state, occurred_at | pk: id | fks: actor_id -> employees.id | indexes: entity_type, entity_id: the reversal's CANCEL audit entry is looked up by the leave_request it concerns; also the trail for the original APPROVED row.; actor_id: who performed the reversal.

table notifications | fields: id, recipient_id, type, title, message, related_entity_type, related_entity_id, status, created_at, read_at | pk: id | fks: recipient_id -> employees.id | indexes: recipient_id, status: unread/read inbox reads per recipient.; related_entity_type, related_entity_id: locate the cancellation notification for a given leave_request (the reversal row's id).

data_notes:
GP-008 persistence slice. One schema change: leave_requests gains a nullable reverses_request_id (self-FK to leave_requests.id) plus an index; delivered as a new knex migration (migrations/<timestamp>_add_reverses_request_id_to_leave_requests.js) following the 20260913000001_add_password_hash_to_employees.js pattern (alterTable add column, down drops it). No other table changes.

Immutability is enforced by the write path, not by the schema: cancelling an APPROVED request performs NO update on the original row — its status, approver_id, approval_comment and decided_at are never written again. Instead a NEW leave_requests row is inserted with status CANCELLED, cancelled_by/cancelled_at set, and reverses_request_id = original.id. Cancelling a DRAFT or SUBMITTED request keeps the existing in-place update (no completed approval exists in those states, so GP-008 does not apply).

Balance release is unchanged and happens exactly once: DRAFT releases nothing; SUBMITTED decrements pending_days; APPROVED decrements used_days by the original's requested_days. The balance row is read with findByKey(..., forUpdate = true) before the write, as submit/approve/reject already do. The release is keyed off the ORIGINAL row's requested_days, never the reversal row's.

Read model: LeaveRequest gains reversesRequestId: string | null; PgLeaveRequestRepository's COLUMNS/LeaveRequestRow/mapRow carry reverses_request_id, and create inserts it (null for ordinary requests). GET /leaves and GET /leaves/:id therefore expose reversesRequestId so a client can tell the untouched APPROVED original from the CANCELLED reversal that references it. findByQuery needs no new filter — the reversal row is returned by the same employee/status/date filters as any other request.

Audit: the existing CANCEL audit entry is still written (GP-002), with entityId = the new reversal row's id and beforeState = the original APPROVED row (unchanged) / afterState = the reversal row. The notification is likewise still sent to the requester.

Repository interfaces are unchanged in shape except ILeaveRepository, which gains findByReversesRequestId(reversesRequestId, client?) so the service can detect an existing reversal (and so the exactly-once guarantee is checkable in application code as well as by the index). All four repositories keep the optional trailing PoolClient and are backed by PostgreSQL via the shared pg Pool.

Open questions recorded: what the reversal row carries in employee_id/leave_type_code/start_date/end_date; whether requested_days is copied or re-derived; and whether reverses_request_id is a partial unique index (database-enforced exactly-once) or a plain index.

open_questions.question: What does the reversal row carry in start_date / end_date / leave_type_code / employee_id — copies of the original, or nulls?
open_questions.impact: Role-scoped visibility (findByQuery filters on employee_id = ANY($n)) and the GET /leaves read model both depend on it: if employee_id is null the reversal row is invisible to the requester and their manager, and if start_date is null the ORDER BY start_date DESC list ordering and the date-range filters silently drop it. Also decides whether the reversal row can be re-cancelled or re-validated.
candidate_options: Copy employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date verbatim from the original (reversal row is a full, self-describing request)
Copy employee_id and leave_type_code only; leave start_date/end_date null (reversal is a pure tombstone)
Copy all four but mark them read-only in the model so no update path can mutate them

open_questions.question: Is the reversal row's requested_days copied verbatim from the original, or re-derived via the shared requestedDays(startDate, endDate) helper?
open_questions.impact: requested_days is the amount released back to used_days on an approved cancellation. If the reversal row's value is re-derived and the original's was ever corrected, the release amount and the original's requested_days diverge — the same quantity would have two sources of truth across call sites (the BR-001 anti-pattern).
candidate_options: Copy the original's requested_days verbatim — the original row is the single source of truth for the released quantity
Re-derive with requestedDays(startDate, endDate) and assert it equals the original's value, throwing ConflictError on mismatch
Store 0 on the reversal row and always read the released quantity from the original via reverses_request_id

open_questions.question: Is reverses_request_id constrained to at most one non-null row per original (partial unique index), or is it a plain non-unique index?
open_questions.impact: This is the persistence-level guarantee that the balance release happens exactly once. A plain index permits two reversal rows for one APPROVED original, which would double-release used_days; a partial unique index makes the second insert fail at the database rather than relying on the service's status check alone.
candidate_options: Partial unique index on reverses_request_id WHERE reverses_request_id IS NOT NULL (database-enforced exactly-once reversal)
Plain non-unique index; exactly-once enforced only by the service's APPROVED-status guard
Partial unique index plus a service-level ConflictError mapped from the unique-violation error code

transaction_contract: Cancellation is a multi-step write and MUST be atomic: the reversal-row insert, the balance release, the CANCEL audit record and the notification are one unit of work. Contract: every repository/service method that must join a caller's transaction takes an OPTIONAL trailing client?: PoolClient parameter and defaults to the shared pool when omitted (PgLeaveRequestRepository, PgLeaveBalanceRepository, PgAuditLogRepository, PgNotificationRepository, AuditService.record, NotificationService.create all already do this). The calling service owns the unit of work: LeaveService.cancel acquires a client via IUnitOfWork.withTransaction (PgUnitOfWork: pool.connect, BEGIN, run callback, COMMIT, ROLLBACK on throw, always release) and passes that client to repository.create (the reversal row), balanceRepository.findByKey(..., client, forUpdate = true), balanceRepository.update, auditService.record and notificationService.create. No repository ever opens BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. The DRAFT/SUBMITTED in-place path uses the same single transaction. Read paths (list, getById) open no transaction and forward no client.
